[09/12/23 03:14 PM] Jordan: +Related to what we were talking about with fundraising, I want to more simply state my thoughts:

- Our 12-18 month revenue growth is highly dependent on the existing services we have
- Based on what I hear from sales I think we should be prepared to run into major headwinds for top 200 customer acquisition in the short term, e.g. the argument we’ve scraped the low hanging fruit

- We have a strong story right now 
- I personally don’t want to get cute with dilution, I believe in the fundamentals of Seso a lot more than I ever did with FBN, but I don’t know how big of a biz it will be. Nobody does. Maybe a few billion sure. But also maybe much smaller due to things outside our control in our industry or slower willingness to pay/adopt modern tech than we’re anticipating
- If we can raise $30m on an up round, it’s actually not that bad for dilution, it takes stress off, it buys us a lot of time to keep building, figuring out how to sell, and determine the right org structure for the industry and opportunity to have a sustainable business or outcome which we’re happy about


I’m not calibrated on any investor conversations or the nuances of our modeling and narrative, but fwiw my gut feeling on this is getting pretty strongiI

[10/06/23 04:35 PM] Michael Guirguis: +2 thoughts I had on a run

(1) let’s discuss when we have enough value added products to commit to pushing a self serve software model that upsells agent services and other things. Maybe it’s managed payroll or payroll, logistics automated on our website and free consulate scheduling (or something else free) if we can 90% automate the application or consulate scheduling or something else 
(2) if we could transition more of our business to pure software we could expand to broadening our ICP much faster whether that’s domestic stuff or H2b or something else. Our biggest constraints are services reputation, price, software capabilities and price. We can subsidize more in the future if we can automate services that other people provide, we can scale faster if software scope is our main driver of growth not visa ops capacity and reputation 
(3) next version of our website (or sooner) should make it really clear that we do not share worker names or data with anyone. Your data is your data, it’s stored securely and you can access or delete it at any time. It’s not even to have this in privacy policies. Like this could even be a pop up that we add to the website and could be in the bottom of our emails 
(4) we are making progress with check but we definitely need to go deeper with the low cost managed payroll option for our customers. I want to deep dive on this sometime this quarter

Parker Conrad 

Compound startups have 5 key advantages 

(1) want to build products where the integration with the other products matter - integration where employee data matters not just HR.

(2) Want to build products where the middleware (platform components you’ve already invested in) matter a lot for the new product 

(3) you have a buyer in common 

(4) areas where things you can do with pricing helps you run circles against competitors

[06/23/24 04:25 PM] Jordan: +There’s been a lot of ad-hoc between us ‘should I fire this person’, ‘maybe we should do a riff’. I found a connection between this 10 minutes and the blurb below by Reed Hastings which could translate to determining how we approach review cycle and who we fire. The framework is, across all of your reports, if someone were to come to you and say I’m going to quit tomorrow, putting aside the pain of backfilling the hand to hand combat the person is responsible for over the ensuing quarter, would you as a manager be relieved? I’m going to start taking this lense and aiming to either fire the person or determine a different role. Or if it I don’t want to commit to firing them but wish there was a more perfect/ideal person in the role, commit to a a coaching/management plan to level up by having transparent conversations with clear expectations. The way I think about where we are: if we’re not optimizing for unit economics with the core filing business businesses’s purpose is to acquire customers and provide an install base for the next chapter of our product and strategy in line with a clear vision, we need to have more structure and effort fleshing out what that chapter two vision is and what assumptions underly it, and then have a concerted effort to intellectually honestly stress test those assumptions and clarify the vision. Legacy Labor is a N of 1 but important example. They’re saying they pay almost nothing for Payroll/HR software and don’t self-identify problems which might require increased software spend. If our entire strategy orients around these types of customers paying way more for HR software than we do today, then digging in and having a POV of which segment we would put Legacy in and what our strategy is for unlocking significant increase in software spend for each segment should be one of the top company goals and priorities that we’re reporting on regularly. The more clarity and confidence we can get on this vision, the more we can creatively consider changes to the business model of what we do, for example lowering our per contract filing prices to acquire more businesses because we’ve modeled what the LTV over 5 years is in a way which is corroborated enough by customer research to align our investors with this approach. 

There’s a balance between the ends of the spectrum at the beginning of this text I try to reach. I have a desire for us to apply more structure to vision/strategy, but also know the reality of startups is understanding that ‘the future is infinitely complicated and unpredictable, and to an extent our strategy is keeping doors open on this hallway we’re walking through because we believe if we stay alive and innovate in this hallway there’s no question there’s enough opportunity for a massive stand-alone business. I may be too far towards the former end of the spectrum sometimes, which results in diving into the micro details, but I do feel strongly one of our 2H’24 goals should be to state a current 2-3 year vision regarding our business model and roadmap and have goals which map to validating and stress-testing this visioniI

[12/13/24 01:38 AM] Jordan: +We need to discuss live but a few thoughts: 

It looks likely we could go live in March with employer api integration. Seso worker app integration I don’t know because they’re building the API, but they’re communicating a few more months of work on their end so conservatively would assume workers are using Dash app until Q3. I think it’s really unlikely we get meaningful revenue from synctera in 2025. Best case scenario (assuming fast approval process) we’re live early Q3 without remittance (could take more time to get that live) and will then take time to get the adoption. 

We need to go deeper on how unlikely it would be employer wouldn’t switch from Dash to Seso but I think there’s a strong argument almost all would if we hand a sunset date where, if they wanted to maintain the same experience workers are using the Seso card. At the end of the day the employers don’t really care so long as they feel the experience is the same and it’s not causing them to incur switching costs. 

I think we’ve been naive about the level of difficulty in building so many products with a small team (even if we’re 30 engineers that’s still not a massive team). I have grown appreciation and paranoia for getting too stretched across multiple product lines, there is so much we need to build for HRIS across permissions, analytics, products to support insurance, applicant tracking, trainings, messaging etc. We need slack and ammunition to invest in big bets whether it be invoicing and payments portal for FLC growers, building piece rate timekeeping, food safety compliance, the list goes on. And every product we add there is maintance and risk of major refactoring. Take onboarding, I’d say there’s a 10% chance in next two years we’ll need to rip out Anvil integration and replace with something else. I’m not saying we can’t or shouldn’t build the paycard product. But if the Dash integration allows us to get all the non monetization value we care most about right now in terms of having a product in the bundle with minimal product and eng investment, I think that’s the right move as it gives us more flexibility on moving faster on HRIS which I think will be much more impactful for revenue ahead of Series C

[04/03/26 07:44 PM] Jordan: +Some initial reactions ahead of going through live on the deck: 
- solid/comprehensive, timelines are aggressive which is good but they also seem tight
- high conviction bets is underwhelming. The features mentioned seem table stakes for any b2b saas co. Theyre fine as foundational infra but I wouldn’t call them bets. The bets are things like agents, payroll clerk, AEWR compliance etc (e.g. things that eliminate work and meaningfully change ROI equation)
- Gap I see: all the research tracks are outward facing (what are HR cos, vertical SaaS cos, agtech cos doing, what are adjacent use-cases we should research like FSC). All useful and worth doing but I’d argue the most important track is missing which is just going and mapping enterprise customers’ back offices and scoring which workflows can be solved agnatically with high ROI. A lot of research has already been done so to start it’s an exercise of compiling/summarizing and then quickly making a call on what new research sprint needs to happen. The FDE workstream should help produce that insight but wouldn’t want it to be deprioritized vs. outward research
- elementum stuff seems to kinda prove the point as they got 15 features from one deployment sitting next to a customer. iI
